questions.enonce_markdown: Describe an experiment to measure the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot. *(9 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Experiment: using a potometer.**

**Apparatus:** a potometer (a capillary tube with a graduated scale, joined to a water reservoir and a tube holding the shoot), a freshly cut leafy shoot, water, a basin, petroleum jelly (Vaseline), a stop watch, a ruler or the scale on the capillary tube, a knife.

**Diagram (to be drawn):** a potometer filled with water; the leafy shoot fixed in the rubber bung at one side; the horizontal capillary tube with a scale at the other side containing one **air bubble**; the reservoir tap; the beaker of water at the open end of the capillary.

**Procedure:**
1. Cut a leafy shoot **under water** (to prevent air entering the xylem) with a slanting cut.
2. Fill the potometer completely with water, **under water**, and fix the shoot into the apparatus with the bung, with no air bubbles in the system.
3. Seal the joints with petroleum jelly so that they are watertight and airtight, and dry the leaves.
4. Introduce **one air bubble** into the capillary tube by lifting the end out of the water for a moment, and put it back in water.
5. Note the starting position of the bubble on the scale and start the stop watch.
6. After a fixed time (say 10 minutes), read the new position of the bubble.

**How the data is used:** the distance moved by the bubble is a measure of the water taken up by the shoot:

$$\text{rate of water uptake} = \frac{\text{distance moved by bubble}}{\text{time taken}}$$

(the volume taken up can be found from $\pi r^2 \times$ distance, with $r$ the radius of the capillary). Repeat 2 or 3 times and take the average.

**Precautions:** no air bubbles in the apparatus; watertight joints; cut the shoot under water; keep conditions (light, temperature, wind) constant; allow the shoot to settle for a few minutes before taking readings.

questions.enonce_markdown: Explain how **three (3)** environmental factors affect the rate of transpiration. *(6 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Any three of:

1. **Temperature:** a higher temperature gives the water molecules more kinetic energy and increases the rate of **evaporation** from the mesophyll cells; warm air also holds more water vapour. So transpiration is **faster** in hot conditions and slower in cool conditions.
2. **Humidity:** when the air is dry, the water vapour concentration gradient between the leaf air spaces and the outside air is **steep**, so vapour diffuses out quickly and transpiration is **fast**. In humid air the gradient is small and transpiration is **slow**.
3. **Wind (air movement):** moving air carries away the water vapour near the stomata, keeping the gradient steep, so transpiration is **faster** in windy conditions and slower in still air.
4. **Light intensity:** light makes the guard cells open the **stomata**, so more vapour escapes in bright light; in darkness stomata close and transpiration is very low.

questions.enonce_markdown: Tabulate the differences between a dicotyledonous stem and a monocotyledonous stem? *(5 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
| Dicotyledonous stem | Monocotyledonous stem |
|---|---|
| Vascular bundles are arranged in a **ring** near the outside | Vascular bundles are **scattered** throughout the stem |
| Distinct **cortex** and central **pith** | Ground tissue not differentiated into cortex and pith |
| **Cambium** present between xylem and phloem (open bundles) | **No cambium** (closed bundles) |
| Capable of **secondary thickening** (becomes woody) | **No secondary thickening** (usually does not become woody) |
| Bundles are usually **wedge or V-shaped**, large, with the xylem towards the centre | Bundles are small, round to oval, each often surrounded by a sheath of sclerenchyma |
